chapter: After the Paradise: club dates and Virginia
title: Teaching Charlottesville schoolchildren after club-date audiences
summary: A professor invited him into his wife's class; he went on to two years in public and private schools, talking to children about their dreams and the real world.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: So, in Virginia you did eventually take a job as a musical consultant...
When I came to Charlottesville, yeah.
You didn't do that al all in Lynchburg?

No, no. But what happened...I knew when I was doing these club date things that sometimes there'd be a lot of children there and the children always used to stand up and look at me. And they'd sit down and just look at me. And then when I get off they want to know my name and we'd shake hands and we'd get to have our little conversation. So, I say, "Well, doggone." Well, I didn't think any more about it. But, anyway, I got to Charlottesville and this particular person, he was a professor and his wife was an intermediate school teacher. And he used to just come into the place all the time and he said to me one night, "Nick, why don't you come over to my school and do something for my wife's class." So, I knew I liked children back in my heart, you know deep in my heart, but it just hadn't come out, you know. I mean the real meaning of it, you know. So I went over there and I said,

"oh, Ill do it for nuthin'," you know, "'cause you come in the club all the time." And he was makin' plenty of money and he was real nice, you know. So we went over there and did it and so he says, "Nick, since you said you'd do it for nuthin', we're going to pay you." And I said, "Lord, umh, umh, umh, there's money in them there hills." So then I did another day and then I did so well, then the public school system, they approached me. And so I did that for two years, the children from kindergarten to 12. Of course the kindergarten children you have to be very visual in order to hold their attention. But I'd ask them what they want to be and then get them up to dance a little bit and sing a little song together and I'd play my horn and everybody had a good time, you know. So what I know in my heart is that it only takes one situation for a child to see or for somebody to say something and it'll give 'em a spark. It doesn't have to be a musician, but they could be whatever they want to be, 'cause I'd ask 'em whatever they want to be, just work hard and you'll make it. And this one wanted to be a veterinarian

and this one wanted to be a astronaut and this one and this one...whatever it is. And then I'd ask them to ask me a question and I told them the reality of life and what the real world is like and, you know, it seemed as though they wanted to hear that, you know. Then I realized that these children have got a little sub-culture, you know, and they'd get together and discuss what I did and this and that and the other and so it got to the point there where everywhere I would go in Charlottesville, if my head was down, they'd say, "Hey Big Nick," and they would say it with such affection and my head would be straightened up...(laughter) And then I did the private schools, too. And then I did...
